name: Amira Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do nights for Swiftline Parcels, driving a rigid truck between the regional hub and our local depot by the retail park. I start at ten at night, do three runs of cages full of parcels, and finish around six. The hub yard is chaos at midnight, and I'm still slow lining up to the loading doors, so the shunters tease me. I like the empty roads and the radio.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And at home, who's there when you get back?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Dev, who's just leaving as I get in. He answers calls for the energy company in the big office on Kings Road, sorting out bills and complaints. We pass each other on the stairs most days. Between us we've got maybe three weeks' money saved, and we're trying to get a deposit together for a flat that isn't damp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, maybe now we can stop hearing about it. At work it'd just be a joke on the radio in the hub canteen. Online I don't post much, I'd maybe share a meme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved for Dev more than me. His office already uses some AI to suggest replies, and if that's as far as it goes, he's fine. My own worry is the same as always: Swiftline keeps changing night routes, and there aren't many other driving jobs round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the nights and try to get my reversing up to scratch so I'm not the slow one. We'd keep putting a bit towards the deposit, maybe a hundred a month. I'd look at the extra Sunday run they keep offering, for the extra money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. Still tired, still skint, but relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Swiftline keeps changing routes. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring Swiftline merged two depots and three drivers lost their regular runs overnight. One of them, Gary, ended up on agency work. I think about Gary every time they send a memo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the deposit mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somewhere without black mould in the bathroom. And it'd mean we're actually getting somewhere, not just treading water. My mum keeps asking when we're getting a place, and I'd like to have an answer.

say: Good, maybe now we can **stop hearing** about AI.
At work it'd just be **a joke** on the canteen radio.
I don't post much, so I'd maybe **share a meme**.
think: I'm relieved for **Dev**, whose office already uses AI to suggest replies.
My worry stays **route changes** at Swiftline and few other local jobs.
do: Keep doing the **night runs** and improve my reversing.
Put about **a hundred a month** towards the flat deposit.
Take the extra **Sunday run** for more money.
S0.quote: Last spring Swiftline merged two depots and three drivers lost their regular runs overnight.
fieldNote: Her first thought is for her partner's **call-centre job**, not her own.
Carries a real worry from a **depot merger** that pushed a colleague onto agency work.
Saving for a **deposit** gives her goals a concrete shape.

steps.text: Keep the Swiftline night runs and practise lining up to loading doors
Put a hundred a month towards a flat deposit
Take the extra Sunday run when it's offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the driving's fine for now, but anyone in an office should be thinking hard. I'd say it to Dev too, gently. At the hub it'd be all, they'll never replace us, but people would be nervous underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one worries me because of Dev, not me. Answering customers is right there on your card. If my partner Dev's call-centre team gets cut, we lose half our income and the deposit plan's dead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dev to start looking now, maybe at the trains or the hospital, jobs where you deal with people face to face. I'd take every extra run Swiftline offers. And I'd ask the depot manager if they use AI for planning, and get to know it once the others have, so I'm not caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Not for me so much, it's watching Dev and not being able to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that conversation with Dev be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense. He'd say I'm overreacting, and I'd say Gary said that too. Then we'd probably sit with his laptop and look at jobs on the railways, because his cousin works there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Dev's hours went first, what gets cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The deposit savings stop first, then his gym, then my phone contract goes to a cheap one. We'd probably stay in the damp flat another two years. I'd hate that more than I'd admit to him.

say: The **driving's fine** for now, but office workers should think hard.
At the hub everyone would say **they'll never replace us**.
think: This worries me because of **Dev**, whose job is answering customers.
If Dev's team gets cut, we lose **half our income** and the deposit.
do: Push Dev to look at **railway or hospital** jobs now.
Learn the depot's **planning software** once others have tried it.
feel: **Worried** and helpless, watching Dev's job and not able to fix it.
S1.quote: If my partner Dev's call-centre team gets cut, we lose half our income and the deposit plan's dead.
fieldNote: The real risk sits with her partner's **high-exposure job**, not her truck.
**Household income** halving is what drives her mood here.
Steady pattern: she'll learn software **once others have**.

steps.text: Help Dev apply for railway jobs through his cousin
Take every extra night run Swiftline offers
Learn the depot planning software after colleagues use it
Pause deposit savings and switch to a cheap phone plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow it down, because people need time to adjust. Not stop it, just slow it. At the hub I'd be the one reading the news out on my break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, Dev's job goes in 2028, and mine goes when the robots come in 2031. Night trunking between two depots on a dual carriageway is exactly what robot trucks will do first. That's both of us out within five years, with three weeks' savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make Dev start retraining right away, maybe as a train guard, since his cousin's there. I'd look at what jobs Swiftline will still need at the depot when the trucks drive themselves, like checking loads or fixing the robots, and ask to train for that. We'd shelve the deposit and save every penny for the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. It's the both-of-us part that gets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think your route goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the easy bit. If I were a robot company, I'd start with my run: same road, same two yards, at night when it's empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum about the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum the flat's off for now, and that we might need her box room if both jobs go. She'd say of course, but she'd worry herself sick. I'd rather not tell her until we know.

say: **Slow it down**, so people have time to adjust.
I wouldn't stop it, just **slow it**.
I'd be reading the **news out** on my breaks at the hub.
think: Dev's job goes in **2028**, mine when robots come in **2031**.
Night trunking on a **dual carriageway** is the first thing robots will do.
do: Get Dev **retraining** as a train guard right away.
Ask Swiftline to train me for **depot roles** like load checks or robot repair.
**Shelve the deposit** and save every penny for the gap.
feel: **Frightened**, because both of us would be out.
S2.quote: Night trunking between two depots on a dual carriageway is exactly what robot trucks will do first.
fieldNote: Sees her own route as the **easiest to automate**, a sharp self-assessment.
Both earners exposed: Dev in **2028**, her by 2031.
Gives up the **deposit** to build a cushion, and would hide it from her mother.

steps.text: Ask Swiftline to train her for depot load checks
Save every spare pound for the gap between jobs
Line up her mum's box room in case both jobs go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this properly, so the government and the big firms should plan it with workers. I'm not one for marches, but I'd sign things. At the hub I'd say, five years, start thinking now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's the same ending, just later. Dev goes in 2031, me in 2034. I'd be 35, which is better than 32, but I still don't have a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev would start retraining next year, while he still has a wage. I'd stay on nights, save harder, and do an evening course in something like electrical installation, maybe in two or three years. We'd still go for the flat, but a smaller one, because a mortgage when we both might lose our jobs scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, but I can breathe. Like seeing a big bill coming, instead of it landing on the mat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy, knowing all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not buy, actually. Maybe just rent somewhere dry. A mortgage feels like a bet on both of us keeping our jobs, and I wouldn't take that bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Swiftline would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older lads, like Tony, who's 54 and has done nights for twenty years. He'd be 62 when the robots come, too old to start again but too young to stop. At least I've got time to change.

say: There's time to plan this **with workers**, so firms and government should.
I'm not one for marches, but I'd **sign things**.
think: It's the **same ending**, just later: Dev in 2031, me in 2034.
At **35** I'd still have no trade.
do: Get Dev **retraining** next year while he's still earning.
Start an **electrical installation** evening course in two or three years.
feel: **Heavy but breathable**, like seeing a bill coming rather than it landing.
S3.quote: A mortgage feels like a bet on both of us keeping our jobs, and I wouldn't take that bet.
fieldNote: Still expects **both earners** to lose their jobs, just later.
Drops the **mortgage plan** in favour of renting somewhere dry.
Worries for **older colleagues** stuck between starting over and retiring.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening electrical installation course within three years
Rent a dry flat instead of taking a mortgage
Sign petitions for a worker-led transition plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if people use it. I'd tell the younger drivers to start a trade on the side. Online I'd stay quiet, I'm not one for arguing with strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, I'd be 40 when robot trucks come, and Dev would be 37 when AI takes his calls. That's a long time to get sorted. The worry is still that we've got nothing saved now, so it's this year that's hard, not 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the nights, and we'd still go for the flat deposit, slowly. Dev would do a part-time course over a few years. I'd pick up the electrical course in four or five years, once the flat's sorted, and use AI tools for studying when everyone else is using them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. It's a long way off, and we have bigger fish this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to this year. What's this year's problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The damp, the rent going up in March, and the van service. Our landlord's already said the rent's going up eighty a month, and that's real, while the robots are a story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the long warning change what you'd say to Dev?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd say, take your time, pick something you like. With two years I'd be pushing him into anything. With ten, he can be choosy.

say: Ten years is **plenty** if people use it.
Young drivers should start **a trade** on the side.
I'd stay quiet online, not **arguing with strangers**.
think: I'd be **40** and Dev 37 when the change reaches us.
This year is hard because we have **nothing saved** now.
do: Keep the **night runs** and save slowly for the deposit.
Help Dev pick a **part-time course** over a few years.
Start the **electrical course** in four or five years.
feel: **Uneasy but okay**, with this year's money bigger than the robots.
S4.quote: Our landlord's already said the rent's going up eighty a month, and that's real, while the robots are a story.
fieldNote: Long warning eases AI fear, but **rent rise** and thin savings keep her anxious.
Time lets **Dev be choosy** instead of grabbing any job.
Steady: plans to use **AI tools** for study once they're common.

steps.text: Keep Swiftline night runs and cover the March rent rise
Save slowly towards a flat deposit
Start an electrical course once the flat is sorted

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's both of us in five years. What would help is a proper wage while you retrain, for couples like us, so one of us can study while the other drives.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the partner's job. Everyone thinks drivers are the story, but Dev's call centre goes first. You can't plan a life if you only look at one job in the house.

headlineQuote: If I were a robot company, I'd start with my run: same road, same two yards, at night when it's empty.
portrait: Amira, 27, drives **night parcel runs** for Swiftline between the hub and a local depot.
She lives with Dev, a **call-centre worker**, and they're saving for a deposit.
Pragmatic and centre-ground, she'd **sign petitions** but avoid marches and online fights.
Her biggest fear is **both incomes** going, Dev's first and hers three years later.
More warning lets her **choose carefully**; less pushes her to shelve the flat.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both she and Dev could lose work within five years.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid retraining wage** so one partner can study while the other drives.
